newsitem.title: USA: No deal yet to give Nazi gold to victims.
newsitem.headline: No deal yet to give Nazi gold to victims.

text.p: The head of a U.S. government task force on Nazi gold said on Friday he hoped to persuade European nations to distribute some six tons of Nazi gold to Holocaust survivors but there was no agreement to do so yet.

Undersecretary of State for Economic Affairs Stuart Eizenstat said in an interview with Reuters that he was hoping to forge a common position by next week with Britain and France, which together with the United States are members of a commission controlling distribution of the gold.
Once those three countries reach consensus, another dozen European nations would need to agree to renounce their claims to the gold, worth some $68 million.

"We're very pleased so far with the positive attitude that the British and French government have shown to try to deal with this contentious issue in ways that do justice to the victims," Eizenstat said.
But he denied a report earlier this week quoting sources close to the negotiations that agreement to distribute the gold to survivors had already been reached.

"There has not yet been an agreement ... We are evolving a position that we will hopefully be able to announce next week. But we do not have at this point consensus among the other countries who have a claim to it (the gold) as to what should happen to it," Eizenstat said.

The six tons are the last of 377 tons captured by the Allies from the Nazis at the end of the Second World War. Two tons are stored at the Federal Reserve Bank in New York and four tons at the Bank of England in London.
Since the end of the war, the U.S.-British-French commission has distributed 371 tons of gold, worth close to $4 billion, to European nations whose treasuries were looted by the Nazis.

But last May, a U.S. government task force headed by Eizenstat concluded that some of the gold was looted from individual Holocaust victims, including jewelry and the gold teeth ripped from the bodies of extermination camp victims.
Eizenstat said the United States believed that most or all of the remaining gold should go to survivors because European states had already received the gold stolen from them.
"Obviously, we're hopeful that our position can be adopted but it's simply premature to say at this point," he said.
Once there was agreement between Washington, Paris and London, Eizenstat said the three nations would try to convene a meeting of all claimant countries in September.
